gao-gaoreports-gao-05-1039t:
Residential Energy, GAO-05-1039T of September 27, 2005, looks at how Washington watches a grant plan that helps poor households pay fuel bills. The Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program sends about $2 billion a year through states, tribes, and territories. A side plan funds test projects that help families cut energy use. Both matter more as fuel prices climb.

GAO tells how the Department of Health and Human Services keeps watch over grant payments. It also sums up a 2001 GAO review of the test project plan. Oversight gaps and past lessons share the page, aimed at tighter grant control.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-1049t:
Globalization, GAO-05-1049T of September 28, 2005, weighs what the U.S. government should do as firms face calls to act well abroad. Trade growth and a surge of cash into poor states raised hard claims on labor, land, and human rights. U.S. firms hire millions of workers abroad. Many run good-conduct plans of their own. Views clash on how far Washington should push.

GAO lists the federal plans and rules that touch firm conduct abroad. It then lays out the main camps in the fight over the U.S. role. The statement takes no side; it maps the ground for the House group that heard it.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-419t:
Military Personnel, GAO-05-419T of March 16, 2005, gives early notes on a wartime strain: to fill the ranks and keep them filled. The Pentagon must draw several hundred thousand new folks each year. It must hold skilled hands in the same span. Three war tasks since September 11, 2001, stretch the force. Long tours and war deaths in Iraq sour both draws.

The facts here rest on work still in train, on troops in the ranks. GAO tells how each arm, Guard too, tracks its draw and hold aims. It tells the tale for hard-to-fill war jobs. It lists the steps each arm takes to lift both.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-439t:
FCC management of the E-rate program is taken up in testimony GAO-05-439T, dated March 16, 2005. Since 1998 the program had committed more than $13 billion to help schools and libraries buy Internet and phone services. Claims of fraud, waste, and abuse by some users had come to light. The testimony rests on GAO's February 2005 report on the program's setup, its goals, and the strength of FCC oversight.

GAO found the program was run by a private nonprofit group with no contract or formal deal with the FCC. Program funds sat outside the U.S. Treasury. That odd setup raised hard questions about which fiscal rules applied. The FCC also lacked useful goals and measures. Its early goals counted schools connected to the Internet, but the data could not separate E-rate's effect from state and local spending. The testimony shows why control of the fund was hard to prove.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-489t:
The Federal Home Loan Bank System, and the changes reshaping it, are explained in testimony GAO-05-489T, presented on April 13, 2005. The system joins 12 regional banks owned by member banks and thrifts. Its main job is lending to members to support housing and local growth. A federal board guards its safety and soundness. GAO traced the system's growth and the hard questions it now faces.

Set up in 1932 to aid mortgage credit, the system changed deeply after hundreds of thrift members failed in the 1980s. A 1989 law let commercial banks join. Banks now make up more than 70 percent of members. A 1999 law then gave the system a firmer, risk-based capital setup. Banks also began buying mortgages from members. Those holdings hit about $113 billion at the end of 2003. Two banks then ran into trouble handling the interest risk. The testimony frames the choices facing the system's overseer.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-519t:
Two fighter programs at the heart of Air Force plans are weighed in testimony GAO-05-519T, given on April 6, 2005. The F/A-22 Raptor and the Joint Strike Fighter are meant to replace aging fighters with stealthy new jets. Together they carry a possible future cost of more than $240 billion. GAO summed up its recent reports on setbacks in both programs and what they mean for the wider fighter fleet.

The F/A-22's case has weakened badly since 1986. Delays and cost growth cut planned purchases from 750 jets to fewer than 180. A budget choice would end buying after fiscal year 2008. The Joint Strike Fighter's plan fares no better. Its development cost estimate has risen 80 percent, and its fielding date slipped 2 years. Planned purchases fell by 535 aircraft. GAO urged a fresh, knowledge-based plan before big production choices are made. More than 90 percent of the Joint Strike Fighter's cost still lies ahead.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-549t:
Overlap in federal food safety work is laid out in testimony GAO-05-549T, presented on May 17, 2005. The safety system rests on 30 primary laws and is split across agencies. The Agriculture Department and the Food and Drug Administration carry the main load. Two other bodies, the environmental agency and the fisheries service, play key parts. GAO summed up years of work on the seams in that system.

The agencies run like work side by side in checks, training, research, and rule writing. Both lead agencies inspect many of the same plants. Some 1,451 sites answer to both of them. At least 71 joint agreements try to manage the split. About a third of them speak to cutting overlap. Yet the agencies track the deals poorly and do not always carry them out. Stakeholders split on whether to merge the work into one agency. They agreed the laws need updating.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-559t:
Another round of comment on the Pentagon's draft personnel rules comes in testimony GAO-05-559T, presented on April 14, 2005. The National Security Personnel System would govern how the Defense Department hires, pays, and disciplines more than 700,000 civilian workers. Draft rules came out on February 14, 2005. A 30-day comment window closed on March 16, 2005. Meetings with employee groups were next on the calendar.

Much in the draft fits sound practice, GAO said. It praised pay bands, pay for performance, and a bigger role for performance in layoff choices.  The gaps are in the detail. Pay, discipline, appeals, and labor relations all lack firm rules. Safeguards against unfair treatment are not spelled out. The draft does not require core skills statements that tell workers what jobs demand. Ten unions had sued over their part in drafting the labor rules. GAO urged that the open points be settled with staff at the table.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-619t:
Emergency continuity plans get a second look in this testimony: GAO-05-619T, April 28, 2005. It sums up a full report issued the same day. Among 23 agencies, listed core duties ranged from 3 to 538 per plan, and some looked minor. Few agencies could show proof they followed sound steps to pick them. Plans had improved since 2002, above all in drills and training.

Gaps persisted: 31 of 45 plans did not fully name the computer systems and data their core work needs. GAO faulted weak oversight by the Federal Emergency Management Agency. New federal guidance and a White House effort may help, if carried through.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-629t:
Transforming defense business operations is the subject of GAO testimony GAO-05-629T (April 28, 2005). Defense took about 51 percent of all discretionary spending in fiscal 2004, even as the budget path tightened. The department holds 14 of the 25 spots on GAO's high-risk list. Its flaws in finance, supply, contracts, and systems waste billions each year and span decades.

GAO names the keys to reform: steady leadership, a clear plan, and honest measures of progress. It backs a law creating a full-time chief management official to lead the change. Without that anchor, past drives have faded.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-709t:
Budgeting by results is the theme of GAO-05-709T, testimony dated June 14, 2005. With long-term deficits looming, GAO urges a fresh look at what government does and how it pays. Grading tools like the Program Assessment Rating Tool can feed that look by tying money talk to program results. Good use needs three things: trustworthy performance data, lawmakers who want it, and coverage across spending, tax breaks, and rules alike.

GAO cautions that evidence will inform choices, not make them; budgeting stays a political act. The testimony reviews how far the grading drive has come under the President's Management Agenda.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-729t:
GAO-05-729T is testimony given on June 7, 2005, about the Defense Department's reuse of excess property. GAO checked controls at selected sites and studied data on excess stock. It looked for waste, poor use, and the root causes of both. It also gathered detailed cases of items lost or misused.

GAO found controls too weak to make sure excess stock gets reused first. Of $33 billion in goods disposed of in fiscal years 2002 through 2004, $4 billion was new or like new. Defense units reused only $495 million of that stock. The rest was given away, sold cheap, or destroyed, while units bought the same goods new. GAO counted at least $400 million in such needless buys.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-749t:
Veterans' disability claims are taken up in testimony GAO-05-749T, delivered May 26, 2005. The Senate veterans panel asked GAO to report on the state of the process. Long waits, big backlogs, and uneven rulings have drawn concern for years. GAO had placed federal disability programs on its high-risk list in January 2003.

GAO said the problems persist. Pending claims rose by about one-third from the end of fiscal year 2003 to March 2005. Gains made in the two prior years were partly lost. Rulings also vary across the 57 regional offices, and GAO pressed for study of that spread. Laws, court rulings, and filing habits all shape the workload, GAO noted. Big gains may be hard to win.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-759t:
The Advanced Technology Program is examined in testimony GAO-05-759T from May 26, 2005. The program funds high-risk research with broad promise for the economy. By law, it must not fund work that firms would do on their own in the same span. From 1990 to September 2004, it funded 768 projects at a cost of about $2.3 billion.

GAO looked back at three finished projects in computers, electronics, and biotechnology. Each had research goals much like work firms had already funded. One was a handwriting system for pen-based computers. Private work on it dated back years. GAO blamed two built-in limits: the need to guard against conflicts of interest, and the need to shield firms' private data. Both make like research hard to spot.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-849t:
Radio tag technology in federal use is reviewed in testimony GAO-05-849T, presented June 22, 2005. The tags store data that readers can scan from a distance. Agencies use them to track goods and gear. The State Department plans them for electronic passports. Falling costs make wide use possible. GAO gave an overview of the tech. It focused on security, privacy, and other adoption issues.

GAO broke the system into tag, reader, and database. Each part raises security questions about keeping data private, whole, and available. Privacy worries include tracking a person's movements and building profiles of habits. Hidden reuse of the data is another concern. Guards exist, GAO noted: risk-based security law, coded data, and tag shut-off tools. Tag reliability, cost, and supply also shape adoption, it said.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-889t:
First responder grants near the capital are revisited in testimony GAO-05-889T, given July 14, 2005. The capital region was seen as a top terror target after 2001. About $340 million in preparedness funds went to the area in fiscal years 2002 and 2003. A May 2004 GAO report made three recommendations on grant management. This testimony reports on their status.

GAO stressed that grants must be used in a coordinated, targeted way across city lines. A joint strategic plan is the first need. A final draft has been completed and shared with key parties, GAO found. The second step, watching the plan's rollout, must wait for a final plan. The testimony also recalls a 2004 finding: a joint governance setup could align spending across the region, if carried out as planned.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-939t:
Regulatory reform efforts over 25 years are weighed in testimony GAO-05-939T, delivered July 27, 2005. Agencies issue thousands of rules each year. Their costs run to hundreds of billions of dollars. Their claimed benefits run higher still. Presidents and Congress have layered reform drives on the process for decades. GAO drew on its many past reviews to name shared strengths and flaws.

GAO found four strengths. The drives raise attention to rules, raise the bar for analysis, widen public input, and open the process to view. It found four reasons the drives fall short. Their scope is limited. Key terms are unclear. Implementation is uneven. And they focus on one stage, the writing of rules. GAO pointed to two avenues for a fresh reform agenda. Both start by revisiting the terms of the existing drives.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1009t:
The 2010 Census redesign is weighed in testimony GAO-06-1009T, delivered July 27, 2006. The count is expected to cost over $11.3 billion. That would make it the costliest in U.S. history. House and Senate bills propose cutting the bureau's fiscal year 2007 request. That raises questions about the design and its costs. GAO based its views on issued work.

GAO covered progress on the redesign, including follow-up with households that do not reply. That follow-up is a key cost driver. It also judged the bureau's project plan and cost data. The title gives the charge: the new approach holds promise. But the bureau needs to build and share a full project plan each year. Only then can costs be watched and controlled well.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1089t:
AIDS prevention funding under the President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief is examined in GAO-06-1089T, testimony from September 2006. The 2003 law behind the plan backs the ABC model: abstain, be faithful, or use condoms. It suggests 20 percent of funds go to prevention. From fiscal year 2006, it requires 33 percent of prevention funds for abstinence-until-marriage work. GAO's April 2006 report tracked funding trends and strains on country teams.

Prevention funds in 15 focus countries rose 55 percent from fiscal years 2004 to 2006. They grew from about $207 million to $322 million. Yet prevention's share of total funding fell by about one-third. Most country teams valued the ABC guidance but found parts unclear. The fixed share forced hard trade-offs against local needs. GAO urged the Global AIDS Coordinator to track the rule's effects. The office agreed to gather data but resisted a narrower reading.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1099t:
Risky federal technology projects, worth billions, are the subject of GAO-06-1099T, testimony from September 2006. The Office of Management and Budget oversees major IT spending across agencies. Its Management Watch List flags poorly planned projects from agency funding requests. A second process, begun in August 2005, tags high risk projects that need special care.

About 300 projects, worth about $12 billion for fiscal year 2007, were flagged as poorly planned or poorly performing. Of 857 major projects, 263 sat on the Watch List, worth about $10 billion. Agencies also reported shortfalls in 79 of 226 high risk projects. GAO found weak data in the funding forms and uneven use of the risk criteria. OMB kept no single list to track fixes or report to Congress. GAO urged better data, steady criteria, and one combined list. OMB largely disagreed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1109t:
Army reserve readiness under long wars is the focus of GAO-06-1109T, testimony presented on September 21, 2006. Large numbers of Army National Guard and Army Reserve troops have deployed to Iraq and Afghanistan. The all-volunteer force must sustain long operations while the Guard also guards the homeland and answers natural disasters. GAO drew on its prior work for this statement. It covered strains on equipment and people, plus the Army's plans to reshape its forces.

Reserve units face deep equipment shortages. Gear shifted to deploying units has drained the units left at home. Units must also leave large amounts of equipment overseas for follow-on forces. On the personnel side, transfers between units and demands for full-time support staff add strain. Two Army transformation efforts are under way, built around modular brigades. GAO questioned whether their equipping and staffing levels will fix the gaps.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1119t:
Mental health funding at the Department of Veterans Affairs is tracked in GAO-06-1119T, testimony from September 2006. VA treats veterans for conditions such as post-traumatic stress disorder and substance abuse. In 2004 VA approved a mental health strategic plan to close gaps in care. The plan called for $100 million more in fiscal year 2005 than in 2004. For fiscal year 2006, the planned rise was $200 million. GAO gave early data on how that money was allocated and used.

GAO reviewed VA reports and spoke with officials at headquarters, 4 of 21 health care networks, and 7 medical centers. Money flows through the networks, which hold most budget power over medical centers. The testimony gives a first look at whether the new funds reached the plan's initiatives. A full report was due later in the fall of 2006. The statement helps Congress judge if added funds match added care.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1129t:
Weather satellites and lessons from past buys are the focus of GAO-06-1129T, testimony dated September 29, 2006. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration plans the GOES-R series, the next set of geostationary weather satellites. Their data feed forecasts, and the series must keep that flow going through 2028. GAO summed up and updated its September 2006 report on the program. It covered the purchase status and the steps managers take to avoid old mistakes.

Other satellite programs suffered cost growth, delays, and cutbacks. GAO checked whether the GOES-R team had absorbed those lessons. It reviewed plans for cost control, schedule discipline, and contractor oversight. The testimony finds that more action is needed to put the lessons to work. Early habits matter most, since fixes grow costly once hardware is built. The statement helps Congress watch a program that millions of forecast users rely on each day.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-179t:
What it will take to make real progress in Iraq is the theme of GAO-06-179T, testimony from October 2005. The United States leads a vast effort to steady and rebuild Iraq after wars and decades of neglect. The work runs amid an insurgency and a fragile political transition. GAO drew on reports from the past three months. It covered the funding spent so far and the three hurdles that most threaten success.

Since 2003 the United States has made about $30 billion available for rebuilding. Other donors pledged $13.6 billion, most of it loans Iraq has barely drawn. GAO named security as the first hurdle: attacks have grown since June 2003. The second is weak data, which hides whether projects work. The third is upkeep; some finished water projects already sat idle or ran below capacity. GAO said all three must be faced for gains to last.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-249t:
Weather satellite troubles force hard trade-offs in GAO-06-249T, testimony presented on November 16, 2005. Polar-orbiting satellites feed forecasters, climate scientists, and the military. Two systems now share that job, with ground stations and four data centers. A single new system, NPOESS, is meant to merge them into one modern fleet. It must keep weather and climate data flowing through 2020. GAO laid out the program's schedule, cost path, and risks. It also described the choices for moving the program ahead.

Technical problems drive the strain. Costs climb and launch dates slip. Each slip raises the odds of a gap in the data that forecasts rest on. Leaders must weigh cuts in the satellites' tools against delay and cost. Some trade-offs save money now but thin the data later. The testimony frames those calls for Congress.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-409t:
Paying contractors bonuses for poor results wastes public money. GAO's GAO-06-409T testimony, delivered April 5, 2006, examines award and incentive fees in defense buying. The Department of Defense spends over $200 billion a year on goods and services. Award and incentive fees offer firms billions in extra pay. The fees aim to spur new ideas, speed, and care.

GAO told Congress the fees are often poorly structured. Used with sound buying practice, they could add value. Used badly, they waste billions, GAO said. The department agreed, in whole or part, with seven earlier GAO recommendations. Readers see what must change in policy and practice.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-419t:
Public housing runs through many hands, and this statement sorts out their roles. Testimony GAO-06-419T, given February 15, 2006, covers the Public Housing Program. Over 3,000 local housing agencies run about 1.2 million units nationwide. The Department of Housing and Urban Development oversees the program. Rents are set at levels low-income residents can afford. A 1998 law gave agencies more freedom and new duties.

GAO draws on its public housing reports since 2002. It explains the roles of the federal department and local agencies. It also covers capital markets and community service groups. Some observers doubt the program's quality. Readers get a clear map of who does what.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-499t:
Tax filing season was under way, and GAO gave Congress an interim grade. In testimony GAO-06-499T (April 27, 2006), GAO assesses the Internal Revenue Service's 2006 filing season and its fiscal year 2007 budget request. Return processing had been smooth so far. Electronic filing kept growing. Telephone access and accuracy improved, in part because call demand fell. Use of the agency's Web site rose, and the site performed well.

The contents also flag weak points. Taxpayers using chain paid preparers may get incorrect help. The budget plan cuts staffing in places. A proposed cut to systems funding could impede future progress, GAO warned. Readers get season results and budget trade-offs together.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-549t:
Part-time service jobs help low-income older workers stay self-sufficient. GAO's GAO-06-549T testimony, delivered April 6, 2006, reviews the Senior Community Service Employment Program. It is the only federal program built for low-income older adults. In 2005, Congress provided about $439 million to serve about 100,000 older workers. The Labor Department runs the program through 69 grantees. Thirteen are national groups and 56 are state or territorial agencies.

A Senate aging panel asked GAO to study effects of the 2000 amendments. GAO tracked how fund shares shifted between national and state grantees. It described progress on a stronger performance system. Challenges for grantees are also covered. Progress has been made, GAO said.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-559t:
The capital region needs a shared plan before disaster strikes. GAO's GAO-06-559T testimony, delivered March 29, 2006, reports on strategic planning in the National Capital Region. Congress asked GAO to comment on the region's strategic plan. GAO had reported on the topic in May 2004 and September 2004. It testified on it in June 2004 and again in July 2005. The topic keeps returning because the region holds the seat of government.

This statement addresses completion of the regional plan. It covers national and regional priorities. It also discusses how to strengthen any plan that is developed. Readers get a status check on joint planning across many governments.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-569t:
The title insurance study reaches Congress in testimony form two days after the report. The testimony numbered GAO-06-569T, delivered April 26, 2006, presents early results of GAO's work on the industry. A House financial services panel requested the underlying study. Buyers generally lack the knowledge to shop for title cover. They rely on lenders, real estate agents, and attorneys. Probes had found practices that may favor those parties over consumers.

The testimony focuses on cost structures and agent practices. It covers effects of conduct found in recent investigations. It also raises the possible need for regulatory change in how title insurance is sold. Readers get preliminary views, with further study to come.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-609t:
Personal data held by firms that collect and resell it is the topic of GAO-06-609T, testimony GAO gave on April 4, 2006. Federal agencies buy and use this data for many tasks. GAO looked at how the Departments of Justice, Homeland Security, and State, plus the Social Security Administration, used reseller data. GAO also checked agency and reseller practices against the Fair Information Practices, a widely used set of privacy rules.

GAO found that agencies and resellers varied in how well their policies guarded privacy and kept data secure. Some practices matched the fair practice rules well, and others fell short. The testimony shows what can go wrong when the government relies on data gathered by private firms. It also points to steps that would tighten those safeguards.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-749t:
Troops' money troubles are covered in GAO-06-749T, testimony presented on May 18, 2006. Frequent deployments to Iraq and Afghanistan strained the finances of servicemembers and their families. Money problems can cost a troop a security clearance or bring legal sanctions. Those risks harm both the member and unit readiness. GAO reviewed what Congress and the Defense Department had done to help.

GAO said pay raises had eased some pressure on military families. Efforts to build financial literacy among troops also helped. The department had tools to fight predatory lenders who target bases, and fuller use of them should help. Still, GAO concluded that additional effort was warranted. The testimony presses for steady support before debt becomes a career threat.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-779t:
A new disability claims process is assessed in GAO-06-779T, testimony presented on June 15, 2006. In March 2006, the Social Security Administration published a rule that reshapes how disability claims are handled. The new Disability Service Improvement process aims at accuracy, speed, consistency, and fairness. One big change would replace the Appeals Council with a Decision Review Board. GAO checked how ready the agency was to launch the system.

GAO found that the agency was positioning itself to put the new process in place. But key parts of the design were still in development. Commenters voiced two main fears about dropping the Appeals Council. They worried that federal court workloads would rise, and that claimants would face added hardship. The testimony warns against launching before the pieces are ready.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-879t:
Clinical lab quality, and whether federal oversight keeps it sound, is the topic here. GAO decided GAO-06-879T on June 27, 2006, as hearing testimony. About 36,000 labs that run complex tests face surveys every two years. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, or CMS, oversees the rules set by the Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments of 1988.

GAO studied lab test quality and the strength of CMS and survey group oversight. Its work rested on a June 16, 2006 report whose title says that oversight should be strengthened. The testimony sums up lab performance data and the survey steps in use. It shows where checks fell short.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-939t:
Undercover tests at the border anchor GAO testimony GAO-06-939T, dated July 5, 2006. GAO agents tried to carry radioactive sources into the United States by car. Most travelers enter through the nation's 154 land border ports. Customs and Border Protection staff run the first check there.

At two sites, the agents got the sources across. GAO told Congress what border monitors did, and did not, pick up in the vehicles. It also noted how inspectors worked through the stops. A fuller account sits in GAO report GAO-06-545R. The testimony gives a stark, test-based view of port screening in a time of high terror concern.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1039t:
A huge U.S. military center in Germany, badly run, is the subject of GAO testimony GAO-07-1039T, dated June 28, 2007. The Kaiserslautern Military Community Center spans over 800,000 square feet. It will house lodging, food, shops, and leisure for thousands of troops, staff, and families. First cost was put at about $150 million.

Work began in late 2003 and was set to end in early 2006. It did not. GAO set out the problems the project faces now. It traced their causes. It weighed what they cost, and what they teach for future builds in Germany. The findings are interim, with more work to come.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1049t:
Anti-poverty deals in Africa, run by the Millennium Challenge Corporation, are tracked in GAO testimony GAO-07-1049T, dated June 28, 2007. Congress set up the body in January 2004. It gives 5-year deals to poor lands with sound policies, to spur growth that lasts. For fiscal years 2004 to 2007 it got almost $6 billion.

The body pledged almost $3 billion for 11 deals. Of that, $1.5 billion funds 5 deals in sub-Saharan Africa. GAO weighed the pace of deal starts in Africa. It set out projects and their run teams. It tracked how fast deal funds flow out the door.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1079t:
Federal costs of Gulf Coast rebuilding are set in context in GAO testimony GAO-07-1079T, dated August 2, 2007. Hurricanes left ruin that forces hard choices on what, where, and how to rebuild. All levels of government, plus private and charity groups, share that task.

GAO placed federal aid given to date beside damage estimates for the coast. It set out the key federal programs that fund the rebuild. It flagged parts of the work apt to draw on federal funds for years. The testimony rests on a coast visit, state and local papers, and talks at all levels. Agreeing on costs, GAO said, is key to the whole effort.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1089t:
Federal watchdogs could be made more free and more answerable, GAO states in testimony GAO-07-1089T, dated July 11, 2007. Inspectors general hunt waste in their own agencies. In a time of rising deficits, GAO sees their work as a prime source of savings.

GAO set out the rules of watchdog freedom, and how they fit these offices. It told how watchdog work can feed into wider federal oversight. It weighed gains from merging some small offices. It summed up a GAO forum on watchdog issues. The statement rests on the watchdog law, audit norms, and past GAO work, and it keeps one aim in view: full audit cover.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1099t:
Two big weather satellite buys are summed up in GAO testimony GAO-07-1099T, dated July 11, 2007. Weather satellites feed data to forecasters, climate experts, and the military. They track storms such as hurricanes, plus climate and ocean change.

One program, priced at $12.5 billion, will swap out two polar-orbit fleets. The other, planned at $7 billion, will replace craft due to fade around 2012. GAO was asked to sum up its past work on both buys. It set out headway made, and hurdles kept. The testimony is a status brief on systems the nation leans on each day, built over years at vast cost.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1149t:
A new visitor center under the Capitol is late risk in a GAO update, GAO-07-1149T, dated July 31, 2007. As of that date, the Architect of the Capitol still projects a June 27, 2008 finish, with a September 22, 2008 opening. Work moves on air systems, stone walls, and ceilings.

Delays hit the fire alarm path, the project's critical path, and most near paths. Cuts to test time bought back some ground, but fire test rules grew more complex on review. New tests for all smoke detectors could add months. A September 2008 opening is unlikely, GAO said, without prompt, marked gains in how the build is run.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1229t:
Health care for World Trade Center responders reached some groups far better than others. GAO testified on that gap in GAO-07-1229T, released September 10, 2007. The statement builds on GAO's July 2007 report on responder health programs. It looks at screening for federal responders run by the Department of Health and Human Services. It also examines help for nonfederal responders outside the New York City area.

The federal responder screening program, GAO noted, had stopped and restarted over the years. It began in June 2003, paused in March 2004, and resumed in December 2005. A total of 907 federal workers had received screening exams by September 2006. GAO said steps to serve responders outside New York were still incomplete. Treatment awards totaled $51 million from the $75 million Congress provided for responder care.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1249t:
The Capitol Visitor Center was years behind its first schedule and still growing in cost. GAO updated Congress in GAO-07-1249T on September 25, 2007. The Architect of the Capitol then expected a November 2008 opening. A contract change had pushed most sequence 2 work to end by November 15, 2007. GAO based the update on the project's status as of that month.

GAO agreed with the November 2008 opening date, though it saw real risk. Delays had hit several near-critical work paths. The cost estimate to finish construction had risen to about $621 million. That sum covered the longer schedule, change orders, and remaining unknowns. About $556.2 million was already approved for construction. The architect had $18.6 million more awaiting approval to obligate. For fiscal year 2008, it sought $20 million more and expected to need $39 million beyond that.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1259t:
Federal executive boards link federal offices in big cities outside Washington. GAO looked at what those boards could do in a flu pandemic in GAO-07-1259T on September 28, 2007. The testimony builds on GAO's May 2007 report on the boards. GAO reviewed 14 of the 28 boards in depth. It chose boards that cover the most federal workers or had recent emergency work.

The boards already bring agency and community leaders together on shared problems. That reach could help in a pandemic, GAO said. But their emergency role had never been formally defined. Funding for the boards was also uncertain. GAO advised the personnel office to define the boards' emergency role with the disaster agency. It also urged clear accountability for their emergency work. A funding plan was part of that advice.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-129t:
Construction of the Capitol Visitor Center kept slipping past its target dates. GAO reported the latest slip in testimony GAO-07-129T on November 15, 2006. The statement updates a Senate appropriations subcommittee that tracks the project. Since the prior hearing on September 21, 2006, work had moved forward. But the scheduled completion date had fallen 6 weeks behind. GAO also covered the expected final cost and funding.

The new completion date was October 26, 2007, GAO said. The delay traced to problems with the fire protection system. That system was the project's most critical activity at the time. House and Senate expansion spaces would finish before the center itself. Both would open together, since final acceptance testing was set to run at the same time. GAO warned that more delays were possible. It flagged thin design support from the architect as a risk to watch.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-229t:
The Pentagon's back-office operations waste billions of dollars a year, by GAO's long count. GAO pressed for deep reform in testimony GAO-07-229T on November 16, 2006. Eight of the 26 areas on GAO's high-risk list belong to the department. Six more governmentwide risk areas touch it as well. The testimony asks whether a full transformation plan exists. It also checks leadership and compliance with reform laws.

Progress varied widely by area, GAO said. The department had built management structures for change. But its system blueprints lagged badly in places. The Army had fully met only 1 of 31 core elements in GAO's framework. Over half of the elements were not met at all. GAO also cited $8 billion in award fees paid out. Those fees flowed whether programs hit their goals or missed them. One satellite program paid 74 percent of its fee while research costs nearly doubled.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-359t:
The Pentagon buys billions in services each year, often without clear terms set first. GAO pressed for tighter control in testimony GAO-07-359T on January 17, 2007. The statement draws on a decade of GAO audits. Inspector general reports add recent cases. It tracks the department's growing reliance on contractors. It reviews how often sound buying practice is skipped. It closes with chances to improve.

Vague requirements are the core problem, GAO said. Work often starts before scope and price are fixed. In Iraq, that pattern raised costs and risks. Auditors' questioned costs stick less often under such deals. In one oil task order, auditors questioned $84 million. The contractor's proposal arrived a year after work began. Other agencies buying for the Pentagon repeated the flaw. Their order files described outcomes in broad terms only. GAO urged defined results before awards.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-369t:
Royalty breaks meant to spur deep-water drilling will likely cost the Treasury billions. GAO gave the early tally in testimony GAO-07-369T on January 18, 2007. A 1995 law waived royalties on some offshore leases. The minerals agency forgot price limits on leases sold in 1998 and 1999. Those limits would have ended relief when prices rose. GAO analyzed production data and the relief laws. The statement previews an ongoing study.

About $1 billion in royalties is already lost, GAO reports. The missing price limits could cost up to $10 billion in all. Renegotiation talks leave the final figure open. High prices make the stakes larger each year. Other relief powers could add to the loss. A 2005 energy law opened new relief channels. GAO could not yet give a precise total. It promised firmer numbers as its work proceeds.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-389t:
Deficits matter, and fixing them will take entitlement reform, spending restraint, and more revenue together. That was the message of testimony GAO-07-389T on January 23, 2007. The Comptroller General spoke at a hearing with that title. The statement lists the fiscal facts first. The nation's condition is worse than widely understood. Its path is imprudent and cannot be sustained.

Better information and budget processes can help, the testimony says. But tools alone will not close the gap. Three moves are required at once. Entitlement programs must change their growth path. Other spending must be reprioritized and constrained. Revenue must rise, ideally through a reformed tax code. None of this happens without bipartisan cooperation. Compromise is part of the prescription. The statement echoes GAO's long-running fiscal warnings.
